Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Mina (Redwood SE), Liam (Arbor Platform), Dr. Priya (Arbor ML), Sophie (Arbor SRE)
Purpose: deep-dive on KV cache eviction, prefetch handoff, long context performance, and on-prem constraints
summary: SE-led troubleshooting retro after an observed production incident: repeated kv eviction during sustained long-context sessions caused CPU/gpu latency spikes and paging to disk. Discussed prefetch/hand-off behavior, hot-prefix thundering, batching interactions, quantization effects on memory footprint, and on-prem/network constraints for VPC deployments. Agreed on replay tests, logs export, and follow-ups for on-prem checklist.
topics: Quantization impact on memory and eviction
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. we wanna run through the incident timeline and focus on the KV side, prefetch handoff and the weird thundering pattern liam reported.
[00:00:12] Liam: yeah thanks Jordan. We saw ~10% error rate spikes and latency p99s jump from 250 to 900ms during our long-context feature test. It looks correlated with a set of prefixes.
[00:00:25] Mina: okay can you clarify long-context: is it user sessions with 30-40 turns or long prompt ingestion?
[00:00:33] Priya: mostly 30-50 turn chat sessions, some with large system prompts included. also some batch-rewrites where we feed prior transcripts as context.
[00:00:41] Sophie: we also had a modest traffic surge + a nightly background job that re-encoded embeddings, might be overlapping.
[00:00:49] Mina: got it. so two axes: memory pressure from long context KV growth (k v cache growth) and burst access to a small set of hot prefixes. that's a classic thundering herd on the hot kv ranges.
[00:01:05] Jordan: can you share the eviction metric graph? I remember it spiked at the same time as p99.
[00:01:11] Liam: yeah i uploaded the grafana snapshot, the eviction rate jumped and the spill-to-disk metric ticked up. attaching link in the notes.
[00:01:20] Mina: quick note: our runtime does prefix-aware prefetch: on token step t if prefix X is hot we prefetch likely KV ranges into the local memstore; handoff to disk occurs when memstore crosses target memory thresholds. if multiple requests prefetch the same prefix at the same time, we can end up duplicating work and transiently increasing memory pressure.
[00:01:44] Priya: is that duplication visible in telemetry? like concurrent prefetch ops for same prefix?
[00:01:50] Mina: yes, we log prefetch starts per request id, but they can overlap within a short window. our dedupe window is 200ms by default; if your burst is within 50-100ms, we duplicate.
[00:02:03] Sophie: our burst was very tight — many clients reconnected after a small upstream retry event so timing clustered.
[00:02:10] Liam: so duplication + long-lived entries equals eviction pressure. but what's causing spill to disk vs eviction-only?
[00:02:17] Mina: spill to disk happens when memstore can't admit new entries due to both total memory cap and per-shard constraints; instead of immediate LRU eviction which would thrash, we proactively spill cold segments to the local SSD page store to avoid repeated re-fetch from remote KV backend. that spill has I/O cost and can increase tail latency if we then read back.
[00:02:39] Jordan: hmm so in your case when the background encoding job hit it pushed the memstore, then the chat burst duplicated prefetches for a handful of prefixes and we spilled to disk which then triggered readbacks for ongoing sessions.
[00:02:52] Priya: are there known heuristics to prevent duplicate prefetches? can we increase the dedupe window or coordinate batching?
[00:02:58] Mina: yes, we can tune dedupe window up to 1s but that risks delaying warmups for genuinely spaced requests. another lever is to make prefetch idempotent and have a single leader per prefix per shard — that's more complex and we can pilot it.
[00:03:12] Sophie: is leader election expensive? do you mean an in-memory token that serializes prefetch?
[00:03:17] Mina: exactly, cheap token but requires atomic compare-and-set on the shard. on-prem we sometimes avoid cross-process elect due to latency and failure modes, so it's often implemented per-worker with short lease.
[00:03:28] Liam: what about batching interaction? our ingestion pipeline batches multiple sessions into a single request to the API. does that affect prefix hotness?
[00:03:35] Mina: yes, larger batches amplify hot prefixes because each batch request touches many tokens from the same conversation. batching improves throughput but raises peak mem usage. there's a sweet spot for batch size and max_seq_len where we minimize thrash.
[00:03:47] Jordan: can quantization help? if model weights and kv entries are smaller we might fit more in memstore and reduce eviction.
[00:03:54] Mina: quantization reduces model memory and sometimes token cache size due to compressed KV entries, but it changes compute patterns — more CPU work per token on certain platforms. on GPU it can reduce memory footprint substantially; on some CPU-based on-prem boxes, lower precision can be slower. we need to run a targeted perf matrix for your hardware.
[00:04:15] Priya: We're on heterogeneous on-prem racks (a mix of A100 class and older 40GB GPUs) so quantization tradeoffs may vary; also our KMS restrictions require keys stay in a local HSM.
[00:04:25] Jordan: noted. separate but related: when memstore spills, do we prefer to evict whole prefixes or individual KV slices?
[00:04:33] Mina: our default is prefix-coherent eviction: we evict entire prefix groups to avoid partial prefix reads later. that reduces read amplification but can make large prefixes expensive to evict. we've seen cases where a single huge prefix causes churn.
[00:04:47] Liam: that's us — we have a few very long system prompts attached to certain enterprise accounts which create huge prefixes.
[00:04:53] Mina: for that we recommend prefix trimming (truncate old history) or store-level compaction: compress older segments into a compact representation that takes less memory and is cheaper to spill.
[00:05:03] Sophie: compaction sounds promising but would that affect correctness for retrieval?
[00:05:08] Mina: compaction is lossless for the preserved tokens; it's just a different on-disk layout. application-level truncation is lossy but acceptable if you only need last N turns.
[00:05:16] Jordan: open question: can we gate prefetch on estimated session WP (working set) size? like don't prefetch prefixes if working set is already near threshold.
[00:05:24] Mina: yes — dynamic prefetch gating based on per-session estimated working set and global mem thresholds is a common strategy. it reduces warmness but avoids cascading evictions.
[00:05:33] Priya: any instrumentation we should add to make root cause clearer?
[00:05:37] Mina: add per-prefetch correlation ids, prefetch latency histograms, in-flight prefetch counts per shard, spill/readback latencies, and an eviction provenance tag (which request caused eviction). that helps trace back which session prefetch caused downstream reads.
[00:05:54] Liam: we also saw an uptick in queued batches on the model-serving side. are batching and kv store blocking on each other?
[00:06:01] Mina: they can if the worker threads block on KV readback synchronously. our runtime supports async background readback where model execution can continue on unaffected tokens, but if the critical KV slice is missing for the next decode step we block. you can reduce blocking by prioritizing critical prefixes and using speculative prefetch for likely next-token prefixes.
[00:06:21] Sophie: speculative prefetch — sounds like guesswork. what are false positive rates like?
[00:06:25] Mina: depends on model and prompt shape; we use small n-gram based predictors with modest precision but good recall. false positives increase mem usage but are cheaper than readback on tail.
transcript_continued:
[00:06:40] Jordan: let's talk about on-prem constraints — Sophie you mentioned HSM and VPC. any network egress limitations that would prevent remote kv backends?
[00:06:48] Sophie: yes, outbound to third-party kv tier is restricted; we prefer local storage or a private peered service. also our storage IOPS on some older nodes is limited, so spill-to-disk can be much slower than cloud equivalents.
[00:07:00] Mina: that matters: our default spill thresholds assume SSD IOPS of X and egress to remote object store under Y latency. on your hardware those assumptions break. we should re-calibrate thresholds and perhaps increase in-memory limits for dedicated on-prem pools.
  [00:07:14] Priya: and what about security — are eviction logs and traces safe to ship? we must scrub PII and ensure KMS encrypts any exported bundles.
  [00:07:21] Jordan: Redwood will provide a scrub and export checklist. logs can be scrubbed via provided tooling; for any sensitive bundles we can use S3 with customer-controlled KMS or one-time secure upload to HSM-backed endpoint.
  [00:07:34] Liam: earlier you mentioned leader-per-prefix to prevent duplication. on our larger deployments that's tricky, we have many processes per node. is there a middle ground?
  [00:07:42] Mina: yes, a cooperative in-process token with short leases plus a small jittered backoff on prefetch attempts reduces collisions by ~80% in our internal tests. it's lightweight and safe for on-prem.
  [00:07:54] Sophie: i'd like to see numbers. can we run a replay with and without the cooperative token?
  [00:08:00] Mina: absolutely — that will be one of the replay variants in the test matrix. we'll capture eviction rate, spill count, p50/p95/p99 latency, and extra metrics like duplicated prefetches.
  [00:08:12] Jordan: ok, timeline: Sophie provides replays by 5/10, Mina runs replay matrix and shares results by 5/12, and Jordan sends the on-prem checklist by 5/7. any objections?
  [00:08:22] Priya: none. also, if the replay shows compaction helps we may accept a small rollout window to run prefix compaction on a few accounts.
  [00:08:30] Mina: noted. one more tangent: quantization interact with KV size — we can provide a sample binary that shows expected memory per token for q4/q8 variants on your GPUs.
  [00:08:40] Priya: yes please — we'll compare to our GPU memory profiles.
  [00:08:44] Jordan: great. any other open risks?
  [00:08:47] Sophie: the replay will identify risks. but i worry about night jobs overlapping with peak — we should add schedule constraints.
  [00:08:54] Mina: we can implement a maintenance window throttle for background jobs that respects global memory headroom.
  [00:09:01] Jordan: perfect. let's do a quick recap.
  [00:09:05] Jordan: recap: root cause hypothesis = tight traffic burst + duplicate prefetches for hot prefixes + a background job that pushed memstore leading to spill/readback and p99 tail spikes. mitigation plan = replay tests for cooperative token + dedupe window tuning + dynamic prefetch gating + optional prefix compaction/trim. deliverables and dates are in the action items.
  [00:09:28] Liam: thanks everyone, we'll get the replays and some long-context samples into the shared bucket today.
  [00:09:34] Jordan: thanks all. we'll follow up in the ticket and schedule a results review the week after Mina's replay.
  [00:09:40] Priya: thanks, bye.
  [00:09:43] Mina: bye.
  [00:09:45] (call ended)
